passage:
So, the Bidisha story. Okay. Last spring Bidisha got the lead on the big client pitch, and I was sure she'd got it by sweet-talking our manager. Not suspicious, certain. I had a whole theory. At eleven at night I was drafting a message to HR.
Then I stopped and asked myself, out loud, like an idiot in my kitchen: "Jasleen, is any of this in you?" And, yeah. I'd been hoping someone would notice me without my having to ask. Saying that took all the heat out.
What I actually needed wasn't to expose Bidisha. It was to tell my manager I wanted to lead the next one. So I did, the next morning, and she just said, "Why didn't you say so earlier?" Bidisha and I are fine now. I even asked her how she prepared.

qa.q: What was Jasleen drafting at eleven at night?
qa.a: A message to HR.

qa.q: Why did the certainty about Bidisha feel so strong to Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen felt jealous and overlooked, and that unspoken wish to be noticed made Bidisha's success look like scheming.

qa.q: What step took the heat out, and what came next?
qa.a: Pausing to ask whether the same impulse was inside; naming it showed the real need, so Jasleen asked the manager to lead the next pitch instead of sending the message.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have been affected if the message to HR had been sent?
qa.a: She could have faced an unfair accusation and felt hurt and distrustful, and the working relationship might never have recovered.

grounding: An adult sure of a colleague's bad motives asks what part of it is theirs, which cools the anger and shows what they really need.

subtype: Hitting a sibling after being scolded [Actor]
passage: In a small Lisbon flat, Mamãe said a sharp "No!" when Paulo tipped his juice onto the sofa. Paulo's lip shook. He turned, stomped over to baby Inês on the play mat and shoved her. Inês toppled over and wailed. His older cousin Hiroshi, visiting for the weekend, scooped her up. "Paulo, she didn't do anything!" Paulo threw his toy bus at the wall, then buried his face in Mamãe's skirt.

qa.q: What did Paulo tip onto the sofa?
qa.a: His juice.

qa.q: Why did Paulo push baby Inês right after Mamãe said no?
qa.a: He felt angry and hurt at being scolded, but Mamãe was too big to be angry at, so the anger landed on the smallest person nearby.

qa.q: What could Mamãe do when this happens?
qa.a: Keep Inês safe, calmly say "You're cross that I said no, but pushing is not okay", and then offer Paulo a hug or a safe way to stamp out the anger.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi see what happened?
qa.a: Hiroshi sees it as unfair, because Inês did nothing, and quickly picks her up to protect her.

grounding: A toddler scolded by his mother pushes his baby sister and throws a toy, sending his anger towards someone smaller.

subtype: Kicking the bag after a teacher's rebuke [Actor]
passage:
It was sugarcane-cutting season in the kasba, and the lanes smelled of jaggery from the crushers. In class, Zeenat Ma'am held up Nitin's notebook. "Look, everyone. This is what careless work looks like." A few boys sniggered. Nitin stared at his desk and said nothing.
At home he flung his bag so hard it skidded under the cot. When Moti, the family dog, came wagging, Nitin shouted, "Go away! Stupid dog!" and slammed the tin door. Moti slunk off, tail low. Aai looked up from the stove. "What happened at school?"
"Nothing," Nitin muttered. Then, after a long silence: "She showed everyone my notebook."

qa.q: What did Zeenat Ma'am hold up in class?
qa.a: Nitin's notebook.

qa.q: Why did Nitin shout at Moti?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and angry about the teacher, but could not show it at school, so at home, where it felt safe, the anger spilled onto the dog.

qa.q: How could Aai help Nitin?
qa.a: Stay calm, let him tell what happened, help him find words for the hurt and a safer way to let off steam, and perhaps speak with the teacher.

qa.q: What is it like for Moti when Nitin shouts?
qa.a: Moti comes wagging and is suddenly shouted at, then slinks off with tail low, confused by anger it did nothing to cause.

grounding: A child humiliated by a teacher comes home, flings his bag, slams a door and shouts at the family dog.

subtype: Snapped at by a stressed teenager [Receiver]
passage:
The first heavy rains had flooded the lane in Sehore, so Ujjwal and Nazia from next door were floating paper boats by the gate. Ujjwal's older brother, Utkarsh, came home from his chemistry exam soaked and didn't say hello.
"Bhaiya, look, my boat went all the way to—"
"Can you shut up for once?" Utkarsh shouted. "Always noise, noise!" He kicked the boats into the gutter and went inside.
Ujjwal stood very still. Nazia whispered, "What did you do?"
"Nothing," he said, and his voice came out tiny.
Later, Amma told him the exam had gone badly. Ujjwal nodded; he understood. But when Utkarsh passed him in the corridor that night without a word, it still stung, and Ujjwal wished he would just say sorry.

qa.q: What were Ujjwal and Nazia doing by the gate?
qa.a: Floating paper boats in the flooded lane.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Utkarsh shouted at him?
qa.a: He felt confused and small, since he had done nothing, and his tiny voice shows how hurt he was.

qa.q: What could Utkarsh do to repair things?
qa.a: Once calmer, he could say sorry to Ujjwal and explain that the exam went badly, making clear the shouting was not Ujjwal's fault.

qa.q: How does Nazia see the moment?
qa.a: She is startled and assumes Ujjwal must have done something wrong, which shows how confusing the outburst looked from outside.

grounding: A younger brother is shouted at over nothing after his older brother's bad exam, and knowing the reason does not stop it stinging.

passage:
Lalit came back from his viva on Thursday looking grey. The external examiner had given him a C, he said, after asking about a chapter that wasn't on the syllabus. Twenty minutes later the delivery rider rang the bell with our dinner, a little late because of the rain. Lalit yanked the door open. "Late again! Do you people even look at a clock?" The rider apologised twice and hurried off, helmet dripping.
I didn't say anything then; Lalit's hands were shaking. After we'd eaten, I said quietly, "I think that rider got the examiner's share."
Lalit put his fork down. "Yeah, Hansa. That wasn't about the food." He went downstairs, but the rider had gone, so he left a kind note and a good rating instead.

qa.q: What grade did the external examiner give Lalit?
qa.a: A C.

qa.q: Why did Hansa stay silent during the outburst?
qa.a: Hansa felt uneasy and sorry for the rider, but saw Lalit's hands shaking and sensed that correcting him right then would only make him defensive.

qa.q: What helped Lalit see what had really happened?
qa.a: A quiet remark after dinner linking the outburst to the viva let Lalit name it himself and try to make amends.

qa.q: What was the rider's experience of that evening?
qa.a: The rider, already wet and a little late from the rain, was blamed harshly for something small and hurried off after apologising twice.

grounding: A flatmate sees a friend snap at a delivery rider after an unfair viva and later makes one quiet remark about the real cause.

passage:
At the Bengaluru office review, Wasim, Eshaan's manager, said in front of everyone, "Your slides look like a college project." Eshaan smiled and said nothing.
That evening in the flat, when his younger sister asked to borrow the laptop charger, he snapped, "Can't you buy your own things?" She blinked and left the room.
Eshaan sat still. His jaw was tight, the same way it had been at the review. "This isn't about the charger," he muttered. He put on his shoes and walked twice round the colony park, then typed a short note on his phone: what was said, why it stung, what he wanted to ask.
Back home he knocked on his sister's door, charger in hand. "Sorry. Bad day at work, not you." Next morning he asked Wasim for ten minutes to talk about the slides.

qa.q: What did Wasim say about Eshaan's slides?
qa.a: That they looked like a college project.

qa.q: What did Eshaan's tight jaw suggest after he snapped?
qa.a: He was still angry and humiliated from the review, and noticing the same tension helped him see the charger was not the real reason.

qa.q: Which steps turned Eshaan's anger into something useful?
qa.a: Naming the real source, walking round the park, writing a short note, apologising to his sister, then asking Wasim for a fair talk 👍.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's sister have felt when he snapped?
qa.a: She was probably startled and hurt, since she only asked to borrow a charger; the apology would ease that.

grounding: An adult stung by a manager's remark notices his sharpness at home, names the real source, walks and writes, then seeks a fair talk.

passage:
During the Christmas holidays we got a whole booklet of maths sums. On the last evening I still hadn't done page six, so I copied it from Keerthana's photo in our class group. When Amma asked, I said, "Everyone copies, Amma. Even the toppers." And Sir sets way too many anyway, right? Who does forty sums in a holiday?
I told myself that all night. I'm a good student, mostly. I help people. So one page didn't count.
But on Monday, when Sir praised page six and said, "Well done, Jagdish," my ears went hot, and I didn't look at Keerthana.

qa.q: How did Jagdish copy page six?
qa.a: From Keerthana's photo in the class group.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish keep repeating that everyone copies?
qa.a: Jagdish felt guilty 😔 and wanted to keep feeling like a good student, so the reasons pushed the uncomfortable feeling away after the copying.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try next time the holiday homework feels too much?
qa.a: Start earlier, or tell the teacher honestly which part was hard, instead of copying and then building excuses.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel on finding out?
qa.a: Keerthana might feel used or annoyed that the work was copied, and uneasy seeing Jagdish praised for it.

grounding: A child who copied homework explains it away afterwards to keep seeing themselves as a good student.

passage:
Lunar New Year had just ended in Kuala Lumpur, and Wei had spent most of it at his grandmother's, eating pineapple tarts instead of opening his history notes. On Monday he turned over the test paper and saw essay questions on topics he had barely skimmed.
By lunch he had a theory. "That test was rigged," he told Omar. "Half of it wasn't even taught properly. And honestly, who cares? Nobody asks your history marks in real life."
Omar raised an eyebrow. "Last month you said you needed history for law."
Wei shrugged and stabbed at his noodles. "Things change." He felt lighter saying it. But that night, when his mother asked about the test, he said, "They haven't marked it yet," and went to bed early.

qa.q: What did Wei do over Lunar New Year instead of studying?
qa.a: He spent most of it at his grandmother's, eating pineapple tarts.

qa.q: Why did Wei decide the test was rigged?
qa.a: He felt ashamed about not preparing, and blaming the test made that shame lighter in the moment.

qa.q: What would help Wei handle this more usefully?
qa.a: Admit plainly that he did not prepare, ask the teacher which topics to revise, and plan a little study before the next test.

qa.q: How does Omar see Wei's explanation?
qa.a: Omar is sceptical, because he remembers Wei saying he needed history for law, so the new story does not fit.

grounding: A teenager who did not study decides the test was unfair and marks do not matter, easing shame now while hiding the problem.

passage:
Mentor's note, first week of the Onam break.
Ganga came by to return a book and mentioned, very brightly, that the exchange scholarship results were out and she hadn't got it. "Honestly, I never wanted it. That programme is overrated. Everyone just goes for the photos." Two months ago she rewrote her essay four times in this office.
Her friend Nirmala, waiting at the door, looked at the floor.
I didn't argue. I said it was fine to feel disappointed even about something overrated, and asked if she'd like to read the panel's feedback together after the break. She said, "Maybe," and left quickly.
Next step: I've kept Thursday at four free and emailed her the feedback, so it's there when she is ready.

qa.q: How many times did Ganga rewrite her essay?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why did Ganga say she never wanted the scholarship?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and embarrassed, and believing the programme was overrated eased the sting of being turned down.

qa.q: What did the mentor do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: The mentor made room for disappointment, offered to read the feedback together and kept a time free, so Ganga can learn from the attempt when ready.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Ganga's bright explanation?
qa.a: Looking at the floor suggests Nirmala knew how much Ganga cared and felt awkward hearing her pretend otherwise.

grounding: A student turned down for a scholarship says she never wanted it, and a mentor gently keeps the chance to learn from it open.

passage:
Tuesday, late.
Aadhya missed the client report deadline again, the one she promised me by Friday. Today she spent twenty minutes explaining. First it was the slow server. Then the client changed the brief. Then, by the coffee machine, it was that I hadn't sent the data in time, which I had, on Wednesday. Each reason was neat and complete, like she'd practised it. "You see, Avni, it really wasn't anyone's fault," she finished.
Weirdly, I wasn't angry. I kept noticing how tidy it all was. People don't polish a story that much unless something underneath feels uncomfortable. Maybe she's drowning. Maybe she's embarrassed.
Tomorrow: skip the reasons and just ask, "Is the workload too much right now?" Then offer to split the next one.

qa.q: When did Avni send the data?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling while listening to Aadhya's reasons?
qa.a: Avni felt curious and concerned 🤔 rather than angry, noticing that the polished, shifting story hinted at something uncomfortable underneath.

qa.q: What is Avni's plan, and why might it work?
qa.a: Skipping the reasons and gently asking whether the workload is too much, then offering to split the next report, invites the real issue instead of more excuses.

qa.q: What might it be like for Aadhya to keep explaining?
qa.a: She may feel embarrassed or overwhelmed, reaching for new reasons because admitting she is struggling feels harder.

grounding: A colleague hears a peer's neat but shifting reasons for a missed promise and reads the tidiness as a sign of discomfort.
